segments.text: You type a prompt, press enter, and the AI immediately starts typing back.
We know how it reads your words, but right before that very first letter appears on screen,
the system faces a massive mechanical hurdle.
How exactly does it decide how to begin?
To see how it solves this, we'll feed an AI a simple question.
What should I name my new dog?
For this example, we will treat each whole word as a single token to keep things clear.
Bridging the gap between fully processing your question and generating the first piece of its answer
is where the real mechanics of AI generation begin.
This board shows the four steps your question undergoes.
Step one breaks your question into tokens.
Step two assigns their sequence positions.
Step three converts each token into a starting vector.
Step four updates those numbers with surrounding context.
This entirely prepares the final token for predicting what comes next.
Your sequence ends with a question mark, which is the final token.
Acting as a collector, it gathers contextual data from every preceding word.
By the end, it holds an updated final vector.
The AI relies exclusively on this mathematical starting point to predict the very first answer token.
Armed with that final vector, the AI calculates a probability score for every possible token
in its entire vocabulary.
It uses the mathematical shape of your question to determine which word is statistically most likely to follow.
Once it scores the options, the system selects a winning token, attaches it to the end of the text,
and then feeds that new, slightly longer sequence right back into the start of the loop to predict the next word.
The AI does not think ahead or plan out whole sentences in advance.
It simply calculates the single most likely next piece of the sequence,
over and over again.
Let's watch this prediction board.
The reply hasn't started yet, so the active final token is still the question mark.
For prediction one, the top probabilities are u at 18%,
a at 14%, and great at 9%.
The system selects u.
The word u is added.
Three more rapid predictions loop through, sequentially adding the tokens could, name, and him.
By prediction five, the reply is you could name him, making him the new final token.
Because of this added context, the math shifts.
The top probabilities are now dog names, like spot at 22%.
It selects spot.
The sentence is complete.
The changing context dictates the flow.
You might wonder why the AI didn't output a dog name immediately.
Starting with u is a standard way to begin a reply.
It's only after building those initial introductory tokens you could name him
that the mathematical conditions become right for a proper name to score the highest probability.
So how does this infinite loop actually end?
The AI keeps generating and evaluating tokens
until the math eventually favors a specialized hidden token.
This is the stop token, which acts as a hard signal that the thought is complete.
Generation is a blind, steady continuation of the text
until reaching that stopping point becomes mathematically inevitable.
This graphic outlines the formal repeating framework for this generation loop.
In step one, the AI ranks every possible next token by score.
In step two, it picks the winner, in our case, spot.
In step three, it adds that newly chosen word to the end of the sequence.
Then, in step four, it repeats the process, using the newly expanded context to trigger
another prediction cycle.
This localized repeating loop, generating an answer one exact piece at a time,
is officially known as inference.
An AI does not write sentences.
It builds answers, strictly one token at a time.
And that entire iterative run is called inference.
